question: How does Cache-Aside differ from Read-Through?

options.text: In Cache-Aside, the application manages the cache itself (checks, reads from DB, writes to cache), while in Read-Through the cache fetches from the DB on miss
options.explanation: In Cache-Aside, the application contains all the cache logic: check → miss → DB query → write to cache. In Read-Through, the cache transparently loads data from the DB — the application only ever talks to the cache

options.text: Cache-Aside caches only reads, while Read-Through caches both reads and writes
options.explanation: Both patterns relate to read strategies. For writes, separate patterns are used: Write-Through and Write-Behind. Cache-Aside and Read-Through differ in who manages data loading on miss

options.text: Read-Through is faster than Cache-Aside because it doesn't check the cache
options.explanation: Both patterns check the cache on every request. The difference is who goes to the DB on miss: in Cache-Aside — the application, in Read-Through — the cache itself. Their speeds are comparable

options.text: Cache-Aside cannot be used with Redis
options.explanation: Cache-Aside is the most popular pattern precisely with Redis. The application calls GET, on miss goes to the DB and does SET. Redis is ideal for Cache-Aside due to its simplicity and speed

question: What is the best way to protect against cache stampede (thundering herd)?

options.text: Mutex/lock: only one thread updates the cache, others wait
options.explanation: SET lock:key 1 NX EX 10 — classic protection. On miss, only one thread acquires the lock and updates the cache. Others wait and read the already-updated cache

options.text: Stochastic early refresh — update the cache BEFORE TTL expires
options.explanation: XFetch algorithm: the closer TTL gets to 0, the higher the probability of early refresh. One of the threads will update the cache before TTL expires, preventing a mass miss

options.text: Increase TTL to maximum so keys never expire
options.explanation: Infinite TTL creates other problems: data becomes permanently stale, memory is never freed. Cache stampede should be solved via locks or early refresh, not by avoiding invalidation

options.text: Use a Bloom Filter before the cache
options.explanation: Bloom Filter solves the cache penetration problem (requests for non-existent keys), not stampede. Stampede occurs for existing and popular keys when their TTL expires simultaneously for all clients

question: When is LFU (Least Frequently Used) better suited than LRU (Least Recently Used)?

options.text: LFU is always better than LRU
options.explanation: LFU performs worse than LRU when access patterns change: if an element was popular before but is no longer needed, LFU will keep it for a long time due to the accumulated frequency counter

options.text: When there are stably popular elements (top products, hot posts) that shouldn't be evicted by random requests
options.explanation: LFU protects 'hot' keys well: an element with 10,000 accesses won't be evicted by an element accessed once, even if the latter was accessed more recently. LRU in this situation might evict the popular key

options.text: When data updates frequently and fresh versions are needed
options.explanation: For data freshness, TTL and invalidation strategy matter more, not the eviction policy. LFU/LRU determine which key to delete when memory is low, not how often to update data

options.text: When the cache is small (< 100 keys)
options.explanation: Cache size doesn't determine the choice between LRU and LFU. For small caches, both algorithms work roughly the same. The choice depends on the access pattern: stable popularity → LFU, streaming data → LRU

question: Which HTTP header correctly configures aggressive caching of static files (JS, CSS) in the browser and CDN?

options.text: Cache-Control: no-cache
options.explanation: no-cache does NOT forbid caching! It requires revalidation on every request (If-None-Match/ETag check). For static files, this means unnecessary requests — you need max-age with a large value

options.text: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
options.explanation: public — CDN can cache, max-age=31536000 — 1 year cache, immutable — don't check freshness. Ideal for files with a hash in the name (app.a1b2c3.js), because when content changes, the file name changes

options.text: Cache-Control: private, max-age=31536000
options.explanation: private forbids CDN caching — browser only. For public static files (JS, CSS), you need public so the CDN also caches and serves files without hitting the origin server

options.text: Cache-Control: no-store
options.explanation: no-store completely forbids caching — neither browser nor CDN stores the response. This is the opposite of aggressive caching. Used for confidential data (banking data, tokens)

question: Which statements about cache penetration are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cache penetration is requests for non-existent keys that always bypass the cache and hit the DB
options.explanation: When requesting a non-existent key, the cache always gives miss, the request goes to the DB, the DB returns null, and nothing gets cached. Every repeated request hits the DB again — the cache is useless

options.text: Caching null responses with a short TTL is one way to protect against it
options.explanation: SET user:999999 NULL EX 60 — if the key doesn't exist in the DB, cache 'not found' for 1 minute. Subsequent requests get the response from cache without loading the DB

options.text: Bloom Filter allows you to determine exactly whether a key exists
options.explanation: Bloom Filter gives two answers: 'definitely does NOT exist' or 'possibly exists'. False positives are possible, false negatives are not. This is enough for protection: we filter out guaranteedly non-existent keys

options.text: Cache penetration and cache stampede are the same problem
options.explanation: These are different problems. Penetration — requests for non-existent keys (cache is useless). Stampede — mass miss on an existing key when its TTL expires (everyone hits the DB simultaneously for the same data)
